properties.name: Bovillae
properties.notes: Bovillae stood 11 Roman miles from Rome on the Via Appia and was the first major stop travelers reached leaving the city. It was an old Latin League town and the seat of a cult the Julian family kept up because they claimed descent from its Alban founders.

properties.name: Aricia
properties.notes: Aricia sat at the 16th milestone of the Via Appia below the Alban Hills and marked the end of the road's first climb out of Rome. The town held the famous grove and lake sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis nearby and was a well-known overnight halt for travelers.

properties.name: Tres Tabernae
properties.notes: Tres Tabernae, Three Taverns, sat 33 miles from Rome where the Via Appia met the branch road running up from Antium. The Book of Acts records that believers from Rome walked out to meet Paul here as he traveled to the city under guard.

properties.name: Forum Appii
properties.notes: Forum Appii stood 43 miles from Rome at the head of a canal that ran alongside the road through the Pontine Marshes. Horace described it as crowded with bargemen and overpriced innkeepers when he stopped there on his journey to Brundisium in 37 BCE.

properties.name: Terracina
properties.notes: Tarracina, called Anxur by the Volscians who built it, occupied a limestone bluff overlooking the point where the Via Appia rejoined the coast after the Pontine Marshes crossing. A temple to Jupiter Anxur crowned the height above the town and the harbor, later improved under Trajan, served coastal traffic.

properties.name: Fundi
properties.notes: Fundi sat on a shelf of the Via Appia above the Fondi plain, sixteen miles beyond Tarracina by the itinerary's count. Horace and Martial both mention it as a stop on the road south, and the town later supplied its own line of Roman consuls.

properties.name: Formiae
properties.notes: Formiae lay on the Gulf of Gaeta and served travelers on the Via Appia as well as wealthy Romans who built villas along its shore. Cicero owned a villa here and was murdered nearby in 43 BCE while trying to flee by sea.

properties.name: Minturnae
properties.notes: Minturnae stood where the Via Appia crossed the Liris river on a bridge just above the ancient port, and Rome planted a citizen colony there in 296 BCE to hold the crossing. The forum, theater, and baths uncovered at the site show a substantial road town rather than a simple waystop.

properties.name: Sinuessa
properties.notes: Sinuessa marked the point where the Via Appia left the Tyrrhenian coast for good and turned inland toward Capua. Its inn, the Tabernae Caediciae, was well known enough that Horace mentioned staying there, and the town's warm sulfur springs drew visitors on top of road traffic.

properties.name: Pons Campanus
properties.notes: Pons Campanus carried the Via Appia over the Savone stream on the stretch between Sinuessa and Casilinum. No excavated remains have been tied to it with certainty, so this point is placed by interpolating along the known road corridor between its two identified neighbors.

properties.name: Ad Octavum
properties.notes: Ad Octavum took its name from standing at the eighth Roman milestone out of Capua on the Via Appia toward Sinuessa. Its exact spot has not been pinned down archaeologically, so it is placed here by that mile-marker distance along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Casilinum
properties.notes: Casilinum sat three miles northwest of Capua where the Via Appia crossed the Volturnus river and met the Via Latina coming down from the north. Hannibal besieged the town in 216 BCE and its garrison held out on a starvation diet until Roman relief broke through the following year.

properties.name: Calatia
properties.notes: Calatia stood six miles southeast of Capua on the Via Appia at the point where the road to Beneventum bent east toward the mountains. Its history ran alongside Capua's own and it lost its independent status once Rome brought the region firmly under control.

properties.name: Caudium
properties.notes: Caudium controlled the narrow pass of the Caudine Forks, where a Roman army was trapped and forced under the yoke by the Samnites in 321 BCE. By the imperial period it was a regular mansio on the Via Appia, 21 miles from Capua and 11 from Beneventum.

properties.name: Ad Calorem
properties.notes: Ad Calorem stood where the Via Appia crossed the Calore river ten miles out of Beneventum on the way to Aeclanum, at a bridge later called Ponte Appiano. No confirmed find marks the station itself, so it is placed here along the known road corridor at its recorded mile distance.

properties.name: Aeclanum
properties.notes: Aeclanum was the chief town of the Hirpini and stood 15 miles from Beneventum on the Via Appia's route toward Venusia and Tarentum. The emperor Trajan had the stretch of road between the two towns repaired, and the site today is an open archaeological park at Passo di Mirabella.

properties.name: Sub Romula
properties.notes: Sub Romula was the next stage on the Via Appia after Aeclanum, 21 miles along the road toward the Ofanto crossing and Venusia. Scholars place it at modern Lacedonia, identified in Pleiades as ancient Aquilonia, on the Samnite border in the hill country east of Aeclanum.

properties.name: Pons Aufidi
properties.notes: Pons Aufidi carried the Via Appia over the Aufidus river, today's Ofanto, on the last stretch before Venusia. Both the Peutinger Table and the Antonine Itinerary record the crossing, and it has traditionally been identified with the bridge known as Ponte San Venere, though some recent surveys favor a Roman bridge further south instead.

properties.name: Venusia
properties.notes: Venusia became a Latin colony in 291 BCE after Rome's victory in the Third Samnite War and grew into a major stop on the Via Appia, 77 miles out of Beneventum by the itinerary's count. The poet Horace was born there in 65 BCE, the son of a freedman auctioneer.

properties.name: Silvium
properties.notes: Silvium was the first stage the Via Appia reached after Venusia on the direct route toward Tarentum, sited on the high ground near modern Gravina in Puglia. Recent fieldwork by Luciano Piepoli has proposed pinning the station more precisely to the Santo Staso area just outside Gravina rather than the older Botromagno identification.

properties.name: Blera
properties.notes: Blera was a station on the Apulian stretch of the Via Appia, 13 miles beyond Silvium on the way to Tarentum. Its site has not been securely fixed on the ground, though Luciano Piepoli's fieldwork has proposed the masseria Castello locality as a candidate, so this point is interpolated along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Sub Lupatia
properties.notes: Sub Lupatia followed Blera on the Via Appia's Apulian stretch, 14 miles further toward Tarentum. Luciano Piepoli's fieldwork has proposed the masseria Caione locality as its site, but without a secure identification this point is interpolated along the known road corridor.

properties.name: Canales
properties.notes: Canales was the last named stage of the Via Appia before Tarentum, 13 miles beyond Sub Lupatia. Its exact site remains unfixed, so this point is interpolated along the known road corridor between Sub Lupatia and Tarentum.

properties.name: Tarentum
properties.notes: Tarentum was the great Greek colony of Magna Graecia on the gulf that bore its name, and the Via Appia reached it 157 miles out of Beneventum by the itinerary's reckoning. From here the road turned east across the heel of Italy toward Brundisium.

properties.name: Uria
properties.notes: Uria, modern Oria, was a Messapian town the Via Appia passed through on its way from Tarentum to Brundisium, a stretch the itinerary gives as 44 miles in total. The split of that total between Tarentum and Uria is estimated here from the towns' known positions, since the itinerary records only the combined figure.

properties.name: Brundisium
properties.notes: Brundisium was the Via Appia's terminus and Rome's principal naval harbor on the Adriatic, reached from Tarentum by 44 miles of road according to the itinerary. Its double-armed natural harbor made it the standard crossing point to Greece and the eastern provinces, and Horace's own journey along this road, described in his Satires, ended here.

properties.name: Dyrrachium
properties.notes: Dyrrachium, modern Durrës, was the Adriatic terminus of the Via Egnatia and the main port linking Italy to the Balkans; travelers from Brundisium landed here to start the overland road east. The Romans took the city (originally the Greek colony Epidamnos) under their protection in 229 BCE and it grew into a major military and commercial hub of Illyricum.

properties.name: Apollonia
properties.notes: This Apollonia in Illyria was the road's second Adriatic starting point, a short march south of Dyrrachium, and its branch of the Via Egnatia joined the main line at Ad Quintum. The city was a renowned center of learning where the young Octavian was studying under Athenodorus when news of Caesar's assassination reached him in 44 BCE.

properties.name: Ad Quintum
properties.notes: Ad Quintum, at the fifth milestone out of Dyrrachium, was the point where the Dyrrachium and Apollonia branches of the Via Egnatia physically merged into a single road. The site is identified with Bradashesh near Elbasan, where excavations have uncovered a Roman villa and a well-preserved bathhouse dated to the mid-2nd century CE.
sources: Not in Itin. Ant. station list; attested via milestone toponym

properties.name: Clodiana
properties.notes: Clodiana was a horse-changing station on the Shkumbin river valley stretch of the road, now identified with modern Peqin in central Albania. A Roman-period castle foundation still stands on the site, and the station appears by name in both the Antonine Itinerary and the Peutinger Table.

properties.name: Scampis
properties.notes: Scampis (Mansio Scampa) sat on the Shkumbin river at the site of modern Elbasan and grew from a Roman trading post into a walled city with towers by the 3rd or 4th century CE. It appears under this name in the Antonine Itinerary and as Scampis or Hiscampis in the Peutinger Table and the Bordeaux pilgrim's account.

properties.name: Tres Tabernae
properties.notes: This Tres Tabernae (a different place from the better-known station of the same name on the Via Appia) was the horse-changing post where the road began climbing out of the Shkumbin valley toward the Candavian mountains. It is identified with modern Qukës in Albania, where sections of the original paved road survive nearby.

properties.name: Lychnidus
properties.notes: Lychnidus, today's Ohrid, stood on the shore of the lake that still bears a version of its name and was the chief town of the mountain crossing between Illyricum and Macedonia. It later gave its name to the medieval and modern city, one of the longest continuously inhabited settlements on the whole road.

properties.name: Nicaea
properties.notes: This Macedonian Nicaea (not the famous Nicaea in Bithynia) is named in the Antonine Itinerary between Lychnidus and Heraclea Lyncestis, but scholars disagree on its exact site, with the Resen basin and the Bukovo pass area the leading candidates. The coordinate given here is a rough placement near Resen, North Macedonia, along the attested road corridor rather than a confirmed excavation.

properties.name: Heraclea Lyncestis
properties.notes: Heraclea Lyncestis, founded by Philip II of Macedon and now an excavated site on the edge of Bitola, was the major crossroads town where the Via Egnatia met the road running south to Thessaly. Its well-preserved Roman theater and later Early Christian basilicas with mosaic floors are still visible on site today.

properties.name: Cellae
properties.notes: Cellae marked the road's passage around Lake Ostrovo (modern Lake Vegoritida) on its way toward Edessa, and its precise site has been argued over since Charles Edson's 1951 study fixed the general area near Arnissa. The coordinate here sits at Arnissa as the best-supported approximate location rather than a firmly excavated find-spot.
sources: Edson, "The Location of Cellae and the Route of the Via Egnatia," Classical Philology 46 (1951)

properties.name: Edessa
properties.notes: Edessa, called Vodena for much of its later history, sits on a bluff over a dramatic set of waterfalls and controlled the western approach to the Macedonian plain.

properties.name: Pella
properties.notes: Pella was the birthplace of Alexander the Great and had served as the royal capital of Macedon before Rome absorbed the kingdom in 168 BCE. By 117 CE it was a Roman colony on the Via Egnatia, and its excavated House of Dionysos preserves some of the finest surviving pebble mosaics from the Hellenistic world.

properties.name: Thessalonica
properties.notes: Thessalonica was the provincial capital of Macedonia and the largest city the Via Egnatia passed through, straddling the road at the head of the Thermaic Gulf. Paul the Apostle preached in its synagogue on his journey along this same road, and the modern city's main street, Egnatia Street, still traces the ancient route.

properties.name: Melissourgis
properties.notes: Melissourgis was a station east of Thessalonica on the road skirting the lakes of Koroneia and Volvi, and its name plausibly survives in the modern village of Melissourgos in the Volvi municipality. The identification rests on toponymic continuity rather than confirmed archaeological remains, so the coordinate is an approximation.

properties.name: Apollonia
properties.notes: This second Apollonia on the route, distinct from the Adriatic city of the same name, stood on the southern shore of Lake Volvi in the district of Mygdonia. Settlers from Chalkidiki founded it around 432 BCE; Philip II later destroyed it before Rome resettled the site.

properties.name: Amphipolis
properties.notes: Amphipolis commanded the crossing of the Strymon river and had been fought over since classical times, most famously in the battle where the Athenian general Cleon and the Spartan Brasidas both died in 422 BCE. Its ruins, including a well-preserved Roman bridge foundation and the nearby Kasta Tomb, lie by the modern village of Amfipoli.

properties.name: Philippi
properties.notes: Philippi, founded by and named for Philip II of Macedon, became a Roman veteran colony after Octavian and Mark Antony crushed the assassins of Caesar just outside its walls in 42 BCE. Paul the Apostle later established the first Christian church on European soil here, and the site's forum, theater, and basilicas are exceptionally well preserved.

properties.name: Neapolis
properties.notes: Neapolis was the Aegean port that served Philippi and the point where sea travelers from Troas, including Paul the Apostle, first stepped onto the Via Egnatia. The city sat on the peninsula now occupied by Kavala, whose old town still overlaps much of the ancient site.

properties.name: Acontisma
properties.notes: Acontisma was a fortified guard post on a hill east of Neapolis that controlled a narrow pass on the frontier between Macedonia and Thrace. Its walls, first built in the 4th century BCE and reused for centuries after, sit about two miles east of the modern town of Nea Karvali.

properties.name: Topeiros
properties.notes: Topeiros began as a Via Egnatia way station and was rebuilt as a proper Greek-style city under Trajan around the turn of the 2nd century CE, taking the name Ulpia Topirus. Its ruins lie between the villages of Toxotes and Paradeisos west of Xanthi, near the crossing of the Nestos river.

properties.name: Cosintos
properties.notes: Cosintos is named in the Antonine Itinerary between Topeiros and Porsulae and almost certainly marks the road's crossing of the Kosynthos river near Xanthi, but no excavated station has been firmly tied to the name. The coordinate given is an estimate along the road corridor between its two better-identified neighbors.

properties.name: Porsulae
properties.notes: Porsulae was a Thracian civitas on the Via Egnatia that later grew into the better-known Byzantine city of Maximianopolis (also called Mosynopolis), sited about seven kilometers west of modern Komotini. In 117 CE it was still known by its older name, Porsulae, recorded in the Antonine Itinerary.

properties.name: Brendice
properties.notes: Brendice is known only from its listing in the Antonine Itinerary between Porsulae and Milolitum, and no modern site has been securely matched to it. Its coordinate here is a rough interpolation along the attested road path between its two neighboring stations, not a confirmed find-spot.

properties.name: Milolitum
properties.notes: Milolitum appears in the Antonine Itinerary as a minor stop between Brendice and Tempyra in eastern Thrace, but like its neighbors it has no confirmed modern identification. The coordinate given is an estimate along the known road corridor rather than an excavated location.

properties.name: Tempyra
properties.notes: Tempyra was the last stop before Traianopolis, sitting just west of the Evros/Hebros river in the area around modern Feres. Its distance to Traianopolis, nine Roman miles, is independently confirmed by two ancient sources that agree exactly on the figure.

properties.name: Traianopolis
properties.notes: Traianopolis was founded by the emperor Trajan on the site of the ancient town of Doriscus, where Xerxes had once mustered his invasion force before marching on Greece. The new city, built directly astride the Via Egnatia, is now the archaeological site of Loutra Traianoupolis near Alexandroupoli.

properties.name: Kypsela
properties.notes: Kypsela stood on the Hebros (Evros) river and was already an old, well-known town by the time Strabo wrote about it, controlling the river crossing on the road into deep Thrace. It survives today as the Turkish town of İpsala, still sitting by the same river on the modern Greek-Turkish border.

properties.name: Syracella
properties.notes: Syracella is recorded in the Antonine Itinerary as a horse-changing stop between Kypsela and Apri, but no modern site has been confidently matched to it. Its coordinate is an interpolation along the road path between its two firmly identified neighbors rather than an excavated location.

properties.name: Apri
properties.notes: Apri (Aprus) was refounded as Colonia Claudia Aprensis under Claudius as a settlement for retired Roman soldiers and became a full city on the Via Egnatia in the province of Europa. Its remains lie near the modern Turkish village of Kermeyan in Tekirdağ Province.

properties.name: Resistum
properties.notes: Resistum is attested in both Pliny the Elder and the Antonine Itinerary as lying inland from Apri on the road toward Perinthus, with Pliny giving the distance between the two as twenty-two Roman miles. No modern excavation has been tied to the name, so its coordinate is a rough placement along the road corridor.

properties.name: Perinthus
properties.notes: Perinthus was one of the great cities of ancient Thrace, a flourishing Samian and Megarian colony on the Sea of Marmara that later became a key communications hub on the Via Egnatia. In 117 CE it still carried its original name; the city was only renamed Heraclea in honor of its legendary founder around the year 300.

properties.name: Selymbria
properties.notes: Selymbria owed its importance to its natural harbor on the Sea of Marmara and its position on the coastal road toward Byzantium, twenty-two Roman miles east of Perinthus. The site is now the Turkish town of Silivri, where an open-air museum displays finds that include original Via Egnatia milestones.

properties.name: Athyras
properties.notes: Athyras was a small Thracian coastal settlement on the road between Selymbria and Byzantium, taking its name from the river that reached the sea nearby. It survives as the Istanbul district of Büyükçekmece; the distance given here is estimated from the known total of forty-four Roman miles between Selymbria and Byzantium rather than quoted directly from a surviving itinerary.
sources: Geographic distance estimated from Selymbria-Byzantium total (44 m.p.)

properties.name: Rhegion
properties.notes: Rhegion was the last staging point before Byzantium, a coastal settlement now underlying the Istanbul district of Küçükçekmece around the mouth of its namesake lake. Like the preceding leg, its distance here is estimated from the attested Selymbria-Byzantium total rather than drawn from a directly quoted itinerary figure.
sources: Geographic distance estimated from Selymbria-Byzantium total (44 m.p.)

properties.name: Byzantium
properties.notes: Byzantium was the eastern terminus of the Via Egnatia, an old Megarian colony commanding the Bosphorus strait between Europe and Asia. In 117 CE it was still an important but unremarkable provincial city of Thrace, two centuries away from Constantine's decision to remake it as his new capital.

properties.name: Segusio
properties.notes: Segusio, modern Susa, was the capital of the client kingdom of the Cottian Alps under King Cottius, who ceded it to Rome without a fight and was left ruling it as a Roman prefect. Cottius's own triumphal arch, dedicated to Augustus around 9 BCE, still stands here — one of the best-preserved Augustan monuments anywhere in the empire.
sources: Itin. Ant. 341 (Item a Mediolano per Alpes Cottias)

properties.name: Ad Martis
properties.notes: Ad Martis, modern Oulx, sat at the foot of the Montgenevre pass and took its name from a temple to Mars raised here, tradition says, to mark a victory over the Cottian dynasty before its peaceful annexation. A small fort (castrum) guarded the station in the later empire.

properties.name: Brigantio
properties.notes: Brigantio, modern Briancon, was the highest station of consequence on the Cottian Alps crossing, guarding the approach to the Montgenevre pass into Italy. Its Celtic name, shared with several other Alpine and British sites, simply means high place.

properties.name: Ramae
properties.notes: Ramae is named in the Antonine Itinerary's Cottian Alps stage between Brigantio and Eburodunum, but no excavated site has been securely matched to it. Placed here by interpolation along the Durance valley road at the recorded distance; the true location may be a few kilometers off.

properties.name: Eburodunum
properties.notes: Eburodunum, modern Embrun, guarded the Durance river crossing on the road down from the Cottian Alps into Gaul proper. Its Celtic name (yew-fort) points to an earlier Gallic hillfort on the same commanding site above the river.

properties.name: Caturrigas
properties.notes: Caturrigas, modern Chorges, gave its name to the Caturiges tribe whose territory it anchored, on the road linking the Cottian Alps crossing to Vapincum. Excavated remains include a substantial Roman-era settlement beside the modern town.

properties.name: Vapincum
properties.notes: Vapincum, modern Gap, was the junction where the Alpine road down from Italy met the true Via Domitia running west to Narbo and the Pyrenees. A civitas of the Vocontii tribal confederation, it stayed a modest town through the Roman period, not formally a colonia until far later.

properties.name: Segustero
properties.notes: Segustero, modern Sisteron, commanded the narrow gorge where the Durance cuts through the last Alpine foothills, the single easiest defensive choke point on the whole road between Vapincum and the Rhone valley. The medieval citadel above the town still marks the same strategic spot.
sources: Antonine Itinerary (Cottian Alps stage, Gallia section)

properties.name: Alabontia
properties.notes: Alabontia was the busiest crossroads station between Segustero and Apta Julia, where the Via Domitia met a north-south road into the Alpine interior. Its remains lie beneath the chapel of Notre-Dame-des-Anges near the village of Lurs, overlooking the Durance.
sources: Antonine Itinerary (Cottian Alps stage, Gallia section)

properties.name: Catuiacia
properties.notes: Catuiacia, identified with modern Céreste, was a minor relay station on the stretch of the Via Domitia climbing out of the Durance valley toward Apta Julia. Roman-period remains have been recorded in and around the village.
sources: Itin. Ant. (Item a Mediolano per Alpes Cottias)

properties.name: Apta Julia
properties.notes: Apta Julia, modern Apt, was founded as a Roman colony under Julius Caesar beside the existing road, its forum and theatre serving the fertile Calavon valley. A 1st-century CE bridge over the Calavon still stands just outside the modern town.

properties.name: Cabellio
properties.notes: Cabellio, modern Cavaillon, sat on the Durance where the Via Domitia crossed toward the Rhone, a Latin-rights town since Caesar's day with its own mint striking bronze coinage. A well-preserved Roman arch still stands in the old town.

properties.name: Ambrussum
properties.notes: Ambrussum, on the Vidourle river between Nemausus and Sextantio, is one of the best-excavated Via Domitia stations anywhere on the road — its Pont Ambroix bridge, paved street with cart ruts worn a foot deep, and roadside way-station foundations are all still visible. Distance given is the itinerary's own figure measured from Nemausus, itself some 30 Roman miles past Cabellio via the road's Rhone crossing near Arelate.

properties.name: Sextantio
properties.notes: Sextantio, at modern Castelnau-le-Lez across the Lez river from Montpellier, took its name from its position at the sixth Roman mile of a local distance count. It became the region's chief town in late antiquity, before medieval Montpellier eclipsed it.

properties.name: Forum Domitii
properties.notes: Forum Domitii, near modern Montbazin, was a market town founded alongside the road itself and named for its builder, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus — the clearest surviving trace of the man the whole route is named after.

properties.name: Cessero
properties.notes: Cessero, modern Saint-Thibery, controlled the Via Domitia's crossing of the Herault river, with a bridge whose Roman piers still support the modern span. Excavated town remains include a forum and baths.

properties.name: Baeterrae
properties.notes: Baeterrae, modern Beziers, was settled as a colony for veterans of Caesar's Seventh Legion around 36 BCE, its name recalled in the legion's own numbering on surviving inscriptions. The Pont Vieux bridge crosses the Orb on Roman foundations.

properties.name: Narbo
properties.notes: Narbo Martius, modern Narbonne, was Rome's first colony outside Italy, founded in 118 BCE the same year Domitius Ahenobarbus built this road, and it grew into the capital of Gallia Narbonensis. Its harbor on a Mediterranean lagoon made it one of the busiest ports in the western empire.

properties.name: Combusta
properties.notes: Combusta, near modern Salses-le-Chateau, marked the point where the Via Domitia entered the narrow coastal corridor between the Corbieres hills and the Etang de Salses lagoon on the final approach to Ruscino.

properties.name: Ruscino
properties.notes: Ruscino, at Chateau-Roussillon near modern Perpignan, was capital of the Roussillon region and gave that region its name. Excavations have uncovered its forum and a large public building, part of it now displayed under a protective shelter.

properties.name: Ad Centenarium
properties.notes: Ad Centenarium, near modern Le Boulou, sat on the last stretch of flat ground before the Via Domitia began its climb into the Pyrenees toward the Panissars pass and the border with Hispania.

properties.name: Summum Pyrenaeum
properties.notes: Summum Pyrenaeum, at the Col de Panissars, marked the exact boundary between Gallia Narbonensis and Hispania Tarraconensis and the end of this stage of the Via Domitia, where it continued south as the Via Augusta. Pompey raised a monumental trophy here in 71 BCE to mark his Spanish campaigns; its foundations were rediscovered in the 1980s.

properties.name: Iuncaria
properties.notes: First mansio south of Summus Pyrenaeus, controlling the Empordà plain approach into Hispania.

properties.name: Cinniana
properties.notes: Poorly localized station between Iuncaria and the Barcino road; the Vicarello cups give a different (12 mp) figure, showing source disagreement even in antiquity.

properties.name: Aquae Voconiae
properties.notes: A thermal-spring station ("Waters of Voconius"); Roman baths have been excavated at Caldes de Malavella, matching the name directly.

properties.name: Seterrae
properties.notes: Minor station on the corridor between Girona and the Vallès.

properties.name: Praetorium
properties.notes: Marks the road's entry into the Vallès plain north of Barcino.

properties.name: Semproniana
properties.notes: Named station on the Vallès stretch; some scholars treat this as an alternate/interior branch rather than the main line.

properties.name: Arrago
properties.notes: Attested name near modern Sabadell; exact placement and route order is disputed.

properties.name: Barcino
properties.notes: Colonia Iulia Augusta Faventia Paterna Barcino, founded c. 15-13 BCE; a major node where the Via Augusta met the port.

properties.name: Ad Fines
properties.notes: A boundary-marker station ("at the border") at the Llobregat river crossing, the traditional edge of Barcino's territory.

properties.name: Antistiana
properties.notes: Sits on the Penedès stretch, bypassing the impassable Garraf coastal cliffs.

properties.name: Stabulum Novum
properties.notes: Attested name meaning "new stable/inn"; no firm archaeological fix, placed on the Baix Penedès corridor.

properties.name: Palfuriana
properties.notes: Precisely located per the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire, at the coastal approach to Tarraco.

properties.name: Tarraco
properties.notes: Capital of Hispania Tarraconensis and the road's major hub; extensive Roman remains now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

properties.name: Oleastrum
properties.notes: Sits at the mountain pass ("Sub Saltu," below the pass) where the road crosses from the Camp de Tarragona into the Ebro corridor.

properties.name: Traiecta
properties.notes: Name suggests a river or lagoon crossing point in the Ebro delta; exact site not fixed.

properties.name: Dertosa
properties.notes: Major Ebro-crossing city and conventus-level town; the road's bridge/ferry point over the river.

properties.name: Intibili
properties.notes: Approximately placed on the coastal-inland stretch through the Baix Maestrat; no firm modern town identification.

properties.name: Ildum
properties.notes: Well-studied mansio, cited also on the Vicarello cups and in the Ravenna Cosmography.
sources: Arasa, "La mansio Ildum de la Via Augusta"

properties.name: Sebelaci
properties.notes: Distances of 24 mp from Ildum and 22 mp to Saguntum are given, but the site itself is not firmly fixed.

properties.name: Saguntum
properties.notes: Famous Iberian/Roman city whose 219 BCE siege triggered the Second Punic War; major node on the coastal road.

properties.name: Valentia
properties.notes: Colonia founded 138 BCE for veterans of the Lusitanian Wars.

properties.name: Sucro
properties.notes: River-mouth station at the Xúquer (ancient Sucro); the river carries the station's own name.

properties.name: Ad Statuas
properties.notes: A modern identification with Oliva appears in Valencian regional scholarship but is not firmly settled.

properties.name: Ad Turres
properties.notes: A genuinely disputed placement on the coastal corridor south of Oliva toward Dénia.

properties.name: Adello
properties.notes: A short 9-mile-pace hop from Ad Turres on the corridor near Calpe/Benissa; no reliable modern fix.

properties.name: Aspis
properties.notes: A name-cognate identification with modern Aspe, inland west of Elche, is suggestive but not archaeologically confirmed.

properties.name: Ilici
properties.notes: Colonia Iulia Ilici Augusta, a major well-excavated colonia near where the Lady of Elche was found.

properties.name: Thiar
properties.notes: A genuinely unidentified station, placed here only as a corridor interpolation between Elche and Cartagena.

properties.name: Carthago Nova
properties.notes: Major Punic-founded port city and capital of the Carthaginensis conventus, with an extensively excavated Roman theatre.

properties.name: Eliocroca
properties.notes: Well-identified inland station on the branch heading toward Baetica.

properties.name: Ad Morum
properties.notes: A tentative identification per regional scholarship on the southern branch of the Via Augusta between Acci and Basti.
sources: AEspA article on the Acci-Basti branch

properties.name: Basti
properties.notes: An important Baetican town on the Guadalquivir-basin approach, well identified archaeologically.

properties.name: Acci
properties.notes: Iulia Gemella Acci, an Augustan veteran colonia and anchor point of the documented southern branch.

properties.name: Acatucci
properties.notes: An obscure station on the mountainous stretch toward Castulo, tentatively placed near Iznalloz.

properties.name: Mentesa Bastia
properties.notes: Distinct from Mentesa Oretana; a genuinely disputed placement near Jódar, Jaén.

properties.name: Castulo
properties.notes: A major pre-Roman and Roman mining town — Hannibal's wife Imilce was said to be from here — and an extensively excavated site.

properties.name: Isturgi
properties.notes: A well-excavated Roman town famous for its terra sigillata pottery kilns, on the north-bank road to Corduba.

properties.name: Epora
properties.notes: On the left bank of the Baetis (Guadalquivir); the modern site preserves the Roman-era name closely.

properties.name: Ad Decumum
properties.notes: A name meaning "at the tenth milestone" from Corduba; placed by distance logic rather than a confirmed site.

properties.name: Corduba
properties.notes: Capital of Hispania Baetica, one of four conventus capitals the Via Augusta is documented to have linked.

properties.name: Ad Aras
properties.notes: A dedicated modern study supports identifying this station with La Carlota, on the Corduba-Astigi stretch.
sources: academic study, "Ad Aras y La Carlota"

properties.name: Astigi
properties.notes: Colonia Augusta Firma Astigi, one of four Baetican conventus capitals, with extensively excavated Roman mosaics.

properties.name: Obucla
properties.notes: A minor town on the direct Astigi-Hispalis road.

properties.name: Carmo
properties.notes: A major hilltop colonia with an exceptionally well-preserved Roman necropolis, on the alternate routing via Hispalis.

properties.name: Hispalis
properties.notes: A major Baetis-river port city and conventus capital.

properties.name: Orippo
properties.notes: A minor station just south of Hispalis on the road to Gades.

properties.name: Ugia
properties.notes: Location debated; placed near Utrera per modern reconstructions.

properties.name: Asta Regia
properties.notes: An important pre-Roman and Roman town near modern Jerez de la Frontera; the archaeological site is well documented.

properties.name: Portus Gaditanus
properties.notes: A port serving Gades across the bay, also cited by Pomponius Mela and the Ravenna Cosmography.

properties.name: Ad Pontem
properties.notes: A name meaning "at the bridge," near the crossing toward the Cadiz peninsula; not firmly fixed.

properties.name: Gades
properties.notes: A Phoenician-founded city (Gadir) and the Via Augusta's southern terminus, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in western Europe.
